'''Jacqueline K. Barton''' (born May 7, 1952 [[New York City, NY]]), is an American [[chemist]]. She worked as a professor of chemistry at Hunter College (1980–82), and at [[Columbia University]] (1983–89) before joining the [[California Institute of Technology]].  In 1997 she became the Arthur and Marian Hanisch Memorial Professor of Chemistry and from 2009 to 2019, the Norman Davidson Leadership Chair of the Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering at Caltech. She currently is the John G. Kirkwood and Arthur A. Noyes Professor of Chemistry, Emerita.

Barton studies the chemical and physical properties of [[DNA]] and their roles in biological activities.  The primary focus of her research is transverse [[electron transport]] along double-stranded DNA, its implications in the biology of DNA damage and repair, and its potential for [[materials science]]s applications such as targeted [[chemotherapy|chemotherapeutic treatments]] for cancer.  Among many other awards, Barton has received the 2011 [[National Medal of Science]] and the 2015 [[Priestley Medal]].

==Early life and education==
Jacqueline Ann Kapelman was born on May 7, 1952, in New York City.  Her father served in the Assembly for nearly a decade before serving as a trial judge in the [[New York Supreme Court]] next two decades. Her father was one of the trial judges in the [[Son of Sam]] serial murder case.<ref name="nyt-1984nov10">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/11/10/obituaries/william-kapelman-ex-judge-and-a-bronx-assemblyman.html?pagewanted=all |title=William Kapelman, Ex-Judge And A Bronx Assemblyman |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 10, 1984 |first=Peter |last=Kerr}}</ref>

Jacqueline Kapelman attended [[Riverdale Country School]] for Girls in [[Riverdale, New York]], where her math teacher, Mrs. Rosenberg, insisted that she be allowed to take [[calculus]] at the boys' school.  Her interest in chemistry began at [[Barnard College]], where she studied [[physical chemistry]] with Bernice Segal. She loved laboratory work and chemical transformations and found Segal an inspiration as a teacher.<ref name=CAEN2015>{{cite journal|last1=Barton|first1=Jacqueline K.|title=A Career In Chemistry|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=March 23, 2015|volume=93|issue=12|pages=15–19|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i12/Career-Chemistry.html|access-date=2 April 2015|doi=10.1021/cen-09312-cover2|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=SegalObituary>{{cite news|title=Bernice Segal, 59, a Professor of Chemistry|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/11/obituaries/bernice-segal-59-a-professor-of-chemistry.html|access-date=2 April 2015|work=The New York Times|date=April 11, 1989}}</ref> During her last year at Barnard she married first year medical student Donald J. Barton,<ref name=Ghaffari/><ref name="nyt-1973nov12">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=November 12, 1973 |title=Miss Kapelman Becomes Bride At the St. Regis |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/11/12/archives/miss-kapelman-becomes-bride-at-the-st-regis.html?pagewanted=all |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |quote=}}</ref> receiving her B.A. from [[Barnard College]] as Jacqueline Kapelman Barton, summa cum laude, in 1974.

She then studied [[inorganic chemistry]] at [[Columbia University]] under the supervision of [[Stephen J. Lippard]].<ref name=Welch>{{cite book|title=The Robert A. Welch Foundation Research Bulletin|publisher=Robert A. Welch Foundation|location=Houston, Texas|issue=56}}</ref><ref name=yearbook>{{cite book|last1=Thompson|first1=Clifford|title=Current biography yearbook 2006|date=2007|publisher=H. W. Wilson|location=New York|isbn=978-0-8242-1074-8|page=[https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2006clif/page/23 23]|edition=67th annual cumulation|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2006clif/page/23}}</ref><ref name=GSAS>{{cite web|title=Jacqueline Barton, Ph.D. '79, and Michael L. Lomax, M.A. '72, to Receive Distinguished Achievement Awards at GSAS Convocation Ceremonies|url=http://gsas.columbia.edu/news/jacqueline-barton-phd-%E2%80%9979-and-michael-l-lomax-ma-%E2%80%9972-receive-distinguished-achievement-awards|access-date=31 March 2015|agency=Graduate School of Arts and Sciences of Columbia University|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402162846/http://gsas.columbia.edu/news/jacqueline-barton-phd-%E2%80%9979-and-michael-l-lomax-ma-%E2%80%9972-receive-distinguished-achievement-awards|archive-date=2 April 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> While at Columbia she began studying transition-metal complexes and their possible applications to chemotherapy.<ref name=CAEN2015/>  She earned a PhD in Inorganic Chemistry in 1979, addressing ''The structure and chemical reactivity of a blue platinum complex: the interaction of antitumor platinum drugs and metallointercalation reagent with nucleic acids''.<ref name=Dissertation>{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302930751/ |title=The structure and chemical reactivity of a blue platinum complex: The interaction of antitumor platinum drugs and metallointercalation reagent with nucleic acids |date=1979 |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Barton |first=Jacqueline Ann |id={{ProQuest|302930751 }} |url-access=subscription |oclc=504880014}} [http://clio.columbia.edu/catalog/2365070 Alternate link] via Columbia University.</ref>

==Career and research==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | audio1= "Nature uses this for long-range signalling and finding mistakes in DNA", [http://earthsky.org/human-world/jacqueline-barton-says-dna-like-a-wire-for-signaling ''Jacqueline Barton: DNA like wire for signaling within a cell''], EarthSky & [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] | video1 = "Science is the most fun in the whole wide world", [https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/dervan-barton.jsp  ''Medal of Science 50 Videos – Peter Dervan and Jacqueline Barton''], [[National Science Foundation]] }}

After earning her Ph.D. from Columbia in 1979, Barton held [[postdoctoral researcher|post-doctoral appointments]] at [[Bell Telephone Laboratories|Bell Labs]] and [[Yale University]], where she worked with [[Robert G. Shulman]]. She used nuclear [[Magnetic resonance imaging|magnetic resonance imaging technology]] to examine the metabolism of yeast cells.<ref name=Ghaffari/> Barton became a professor of chemistry at Hunter College from 1980 to 1982, and began to develop her own laboratory, the Barton Research Group.<ref name=Ghaffari/> While at Hunter, she studied the interactions of zinc ions with DNA, and later the interactions of ruthenium(II) and cobalt(III) complexes with DNA. This enabled her to roughly model complexes on a DNA helix and to begin studying the photophysical and photochemical properties related to [[enantiomers]].<ref name=CAEN2015/>

In the 1980s, she moved to Columbia University where she taught from 1983 to 1989.<ref name=Ghaffari/>  She became a full professor in 1986<ref name=Wilson2015>{{cite journal|last1=Wilson|first1=Elizabeth K.|title=Jacqueline Barton Named Priestley Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=June 12, 2014|volume=92|issue=24|page=4|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/92/i24/Jacqueline-Barton-Named-Priestley-Medalist.html|access-date=2 April 2015|doi=10.1021/cen-09224-notw1|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and was the first woman to receive tenure in the chemistry department at Columbia.<ref name=CAEN2015/> Her research focused on the use of organo-[[ruthenium]] complexes to examine the physical structure of DNA. With [[Nicholas Turro]] and Vijay Kumar she studied the interactions of ruthenium phenanthroline complexes and DNA and was able to design binding molecules targeted to specific DNA sequences.<ref name=CAEN2015/> Photosensitive ruthenium complexes would glow brightly when they attached to the DNA double helix. When rhodium complexes were attached to the DNA, they would attract the electron causing the glow, and "turn off" the effect.  During her time at Columbia, Barton obtained two patents for this method of analyzing DNA structure.<ref name=light/>

In 1989, Barton moved to [[Caltech]],<ref name=Wilson2015/> where her research has focused on charge transport in DNA. By using specially designed chiral metal complexes as probes of DNA she has been able to study how DNA is damaged and repaired.<ref name=Wilson2015/>  In DNA-based diagnostic tests, complexes are used to determine whether electrons can flow across the DNA. If an electron could not move along the DNA, the DNA would continue to glow, indicating that there was damage in the DNA genetic molecule.<ref name=light/>

The research that Barton, [[Catherine J. Murphy]], Megan Núñez and others have done at Caltech has supported the idea of fast long-range electron transfer over DNA, challenging accepted scientific views and causing considerable controversy.<ref name=CAEN2015/> Based on years of studies, Barton and her group theorize that DNA operates like a wire, supporting a type of long-range signaling that enables repair proteins to detect and correct mistakes in DNA. This view of DNA is deeper and more dynamic than previous views of DNA as a static library.<ref name=EarthSky/>

Understanding the mediation of electron-transfer chemistry by the DNA double helix has laid a foundation for the development of new diagnostic tools and for the possible design of novel chemotherapeutics.<ref name=CAEN2015/><ref name=AICGold/>  Barton, Erik Holmlin, Shana Kelley, and Mike Hill created the company GeneOhm Sciences to explore the development of sensitive diagnostics for detecting DNA mismatches.  The company has since been acquired by [[Becton Dickinson|BD Diagnostics]].<ref name=CAEN2015/>

Barton has taught more than 100 graduate and postdoctoral students, many of whom are women.<ref name=AICGold/> Recognized as a "superb role model, not just for young women but for all young scientists",<ref name=Wilson2015/> Barton advises others that "the best thing that I can do for women in science is first to do good science".<ref name=CAEN2015/>  She became the Arthur and Marian Hanisch Memorial Professor of Chemistry in 1997.<ref name=Bloomberg>{{cite news|title=Jacqueline K. Barton Ph.D.|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=1135245|access-date=3 April 2015|work=Bloomberg Business}}</ref>  She was named chair of the Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering of [[California Institute of Technology]], effective July 1, 2009.<ref name=Ghaffari>{{cite book|last1=Ghaffari|first1=Elizabeth|title=Women Leaders at Work: Untold Tales of Women Achieving Their Ambitions|date=2011|publisher=Apress|isbn=978-1-4302-3730-3|pages=115–124|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwpxyTC-QU4C&pg=PA115}}</ref>

Barton was a Member of the Board of Directors of [[Dow Chemical]] for more than twenty years.<ref name=DowBio>{{cite web|title=Jacqueline K. Barton|url=http://www.dow.com/investors/corpgov/leader/barton.htm|website=Dow|access-date=31 March 2015}}</ref> She has also served on the [[Gilead Sciences]] Scientific Advisory Board (1989–2008) and has been a member of Gilead's Board of Directors since 2018.<ref name=Ghaffari/>

In 1990, she married [[Peter Dervan]], a fellow chemist and professor at Caltech,<ref name=Priestley2015>{{cite journal|title=Meet Jacqueline K. Barton, 2015 Priestley Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=Mar 23, 2015|volume=93|issue=12|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i12/Meet-Jaqueline-K-Barton-2015.html|access-date=2 April 2015}}</ref> who is also a National Medal of Science winner.<ref name=NSF2011>{{cite news|title=President Obama Honors Nation's Top Scientists and Innovators|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=121840|access-date=3 April 2015|work=National Science Foundation|date=October 14, 2011}}</ref> She has two children, a daughter, Elizabeth (born in 1991),<ref name=NYT2004/> and a stepson Andrew.<ref name=NYT2004/>

===Research summary===
[[File:National Medal of Science 2010 recipients.jpg|thumb|250px|Barton (third right) receiving the National Medal of Science at the White House in 2011]]
Barton introduced the application of transition metal complexes to probe recognition and reactions of double helical DNA. She has designed chiral metal complexes which mimic the properties of DNA-binding proteins, allowing other researchers the capability to simulate and analyze experiments in this nature. Barton additionally established that DNA charge transport chemistry is extremely sensitive to intervening perturbations in the DNA base stack, as with single base mismatches or lesions. This discovery has been a cornerstone for the development of DNA-based electrochemical sensors.

==Awards and honors==
Barton was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]] by [[Barack Obama]] in 2011, "For discovery of a new property of the DNA helix, long-range electron transfer, and for showing that electron transfer depends upon stacking of the base pairs and DNA dynamics.  Her experiments reveal a strategy for how DNA repair proteins locate DNA lesions and demonstrate a biological role for DNA-mediated charge transfer."<ref name=WhiteHouse2011>{{cite news|title=President Obama Honors Nation's Top Scientists and Innovators|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2011/09/27/president-obama-honors-nation-s-top-scientists-and-innovators|access-date=2 April 2015|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|date=September 27, 2011}}</ref> Other awards include:
